pedagogy.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not a digit-counting one: the digit in the highest place decides the size, so you compare tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths — exactly as with whole numbers you compare from the left. The whole difficulty is that decimals invite false analogies with whole numbers. Two opposite faulty rules dominate: 'longer-is-larger' (0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a separate whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (0.4 > 0.87, either because 0.4 is read like 1/4 versus 1/87, or from the partial truth 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach comparison through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.
bestPractices: Compare from the highest place value: line up the points, compare tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — and reason aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths').
Use ragged decimals deliberately (0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11) because same-length pairs let faulty rules pass undetected.
Establish annexing zeros as value-preserving: 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700, so you may fill to equal length to compare — but only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute.
Use a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) or a number line where size is shown by length, which is conceptually clearer than area/volume blocks, so 0.38 is visibly shorter than 0.4.

Name the misconception to be resisted (metacognitive approach) and show correct and incorrect comparisons side by side, since the error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method — rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and mask the misconception.
keyRepresentations: Place-value chart with decimals aligned on the point
Number line (with zoom) for locating and comparing ragged decimals
Linear Arithmetic Blocks / length model where size = length
10×10 hundredths grids shaded for each decimal to compare area
Side-by-side correct vs incorrect comparison cards for discussion
commonMisconceptions: Longer-is-larger: judging the decimal with more digits as larger (0.45 > 0.5, 0.311 > 0.4), treating the tail as a whole number.
Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 0.4 > 0.87 because 0.4 is read as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87 ('sharing among fewer gives more').
Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 0.4 > 0.87 from the over-applied partial truth that a tenth is bigger than a hundredth.
Believing annexing a zero changes value (0.7 ≠ 0.70).
Comparing digit-by-digit from the right, or comparing the fractional parts as isolated whole numbers regardless of place.

learn.summary: Comparing decimals is a place-value skill, not digit-counting. You compare from the highest place: any whole-number part first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, until the digits differ, reasoning aloud ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, which is less than 4 tenths'). The core difficulty is false analogy with whole numbers, producing two opposite faulty rules: 'longer-is-larger' (claiming 0.45 > 0.5 'because 45 > 5', treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger' (claiming 0.4 > 0.87, from reading 0.4 as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87, or from over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'). Both faulty rules give correct answers on tidy same-length pairs, so RAGGED decimals (different numbers of places) are essential to expose them. Teach through place-value reasoning and a length model, and establish that annexing zeros (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) does not change value.

activities.title: Order ragged decimals against a length model
feedback: If the learner ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'), draw the bars: 0.38 is plainly shorter than 0.4, and 0.312 is shortest. Say in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths.'

If the learner picks the shorter decimal as larger using a sharing/fraction analogy on 0.4 vs 0.87 ('like 1/4 vs 1/87'), separate decimal place value from denominator size: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is larger; show both lengths.
If the learner says 'tenths beat hundredths so 0.4 > 0.87', compare from the left: 0.87 already has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter.

If the learner ranks 0.405 above 0.45 because '405 > 45', line up the points: both have 4 tenths, then 0.45 has 5 hundredths while 0.405 has 0 hundredths, so 0.45 is larger — the extra digits in 0.405 are thousandths, not a bigger whole number.
If the learner says 0.7 and 0.70 differ, show seven tenths equals seventy hundredths and the two lengths are identical.
When the learner reasons highest-place-first and justifies in place-value words, confirm the method and extend to a new thousandths case, for example ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2.
activities.rationale: Two opposite, documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison, and both pass on same-length pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model and place-value reasoning are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'. Predicting-then-checking against visible length is intended to confront the longer-is-larger error at the moment the whole-number rule breaks. The main set already exposes longer-is-larger but can hide shorter-is-larger, so 0.4 vs 0.87 is needed to surface shorter-is-larger, while 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 give further checks on longer-is-larger.
sourceClaims: Two opposite, well-documented misconceptions dominate decimal comparison — 'longer-is-larger' (more digits taken as larger, treating the tail as a whole number) and 'shorter-is-larger', the latter with two sub-types: confusing decimals with fractions (0.4 read as 1/4 vs 0.87 as 1/87) and over-applying 'tenths are bigger than hundredths'. Faulty strategies can yield correct answers on tidy pairs, so ragged decimals are needed to expose them; a length model (Linear Arithmetic Blocks) and place-value reasoning ('0.38 is 3 tenths and 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths') are recommended over rote 'add zeros and compare as whole numbers'.
learnerActions: Before using any model, predict the order of ragged decimals from smallest to largest and say why, e.g. for 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5.
Represent each decimal as a bar or length drawn to a common scale (for example a Linear Arithmetic Block / bar model), then check your predicted order against the lengths.

State the correct order (0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5) and justify it in place-value language: 0.312 and 0.38 both have 3 tenths, so they are smaller than 0.4 (4 tenths) and 0.5 (5 tenths); among the 3-tenths numbers, 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths).

Also compare the counterexample ragged pairs 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11, and 0.45 vs 0.405: predict first, then check each against the length model and in place-value words. These pairs deliberately trip both faulty rules — for example 0.45 vs 0.405 tempts longer-is-larger (405 looks bigger than 45), yet 0.45 (4 tenths 5 hundredths) is larger than 0.405 (4 tenths 0 hundredths 5 thousandths); and on the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 set a shorter-is-larger learner can still land the right order.
Locate the decimals on a number line and, where helpful, zoom between 0.3 and 0.4 to see 0.38 and 0.312 separated in the hundredths.
Compare 0.7 with 0.70 (optionally using an annex-zero toggle or shading) and explain why trailing zeros do not change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: The decimal with more digits is not automatically larger, and the one with fewer digits is not automatically larger either; size is decided by the highest place where the digits differ. A length/number-line model shows that more digits need not mean more length (0.38 is shorter than 0.4, but 0.87 is longer than 0.4). Annexing trailing zeros gives decimals the same number of decimal places without changing their value.

activities.title: Name and resist the whole-number rule (correct vs incorrect cards)
feedback: If the learner cannot name why a wrong card is wrong, re-read both decimals in place-value words and point to where the comparison first decides (the highest differing place).
Praise explicit self-monitoring ('I nearly counted the digits — but I compared tenths first').
If the learner only identifies the right answer without naming the faulty rule, prompt: which rule would make someone pick the wrong card here?
activities.rationale: The greater-digits misconception reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge and is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended.
sourceClaims: The 'greater number of digits means greater magnitude' misconception is among the most common in decimal comparison and reflects an overgeneralisation of whole-number knowledge; it is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, so metacognitive approaches that name the misconception and present correct/incorrect examples side by side are recommended. Longer-is-larger declines with age while shorter-is-larger persists into adulthood.
learnerActions: Look at side-by-side comparison cards, one clearly labelled correct and one clearly labelled wrong, e.g. '0.45 > 0.5' (labelled wrong) beside '0.45 < 0.5' (labelled correct).
Say out loud which faulty rule produced the wrong card ('longer-is-larger: it counted 45 against 5') and explain why it fails here.
Write or state the place-value reason the correct card holds (0.5 is 5 tenths; 0.45 is 4 tenths 5 hundredths; 5 tenths is more).
Before answering each new pair, flag the rule you must NOT use, then compare correctly.
activities.intendedInsight: The error is partly a failure to inhibit the whole-number rule, not only missing knowledge; naming the misconception and inspecting clearly-labelled correct/incorrect examples side by side helps a learner catch and override it.

activities.title: Show equivalence and area with hundredths grids
feedback: If the learner thinks 0.38 covers more than 0.4 because '38 > 4', count tenths columns: 0.4 fills four full columns (40 squares), 0.38 fills three columns and part of a fourth (38 squares).
If the learner denies 0.7 = 0.70, overlay or count: 7 tenths = 70 hundredths cover the same squares.
On the aligned chart, if the learner compares from the right, redirect to the highest place first.
activities.rationale: Grids and an aligned place-value chart are useful references for area comparison and for making annexing-zeros equivalence concrete; however such references need to be paired with practice across many ragged cases with feedback rather than used alone.
learnerActions: Shade 0.4 and 0.38 each on a 10×10 hundredths grid and compare the shaded areas.
Shade 0.7 on one grid and 0.70 on another, and explain why seven tenths fills the same area as seventy hundredths.
Use an aligned place-value chart (points lined up) to read each decimal digit by digit, starting from tenths, and state which decimal is larger and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Decimals can be compared by area as well as by length, and both representations show that annexing a zero (0.7 = 0.70) preserves value while more digits need not mean more size. (Note: the source synthesis treats length as the clearest magnitude model for this topic; the grid is a complementary reference.)

constraints: Use ragged decimals deliberately (e.g. 0.4 vs 0.38, 0.5 vs 0.45, 0.9 vs 0.11, 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.45 vs 0.405); same-length pairs let both faulty rules pass undetected and should not be the only practice.
On the 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 ordering set a shorter-is-larger learner can still reach the right order, so include at least one pair (such as 0.4 vs 0.87) that directly exposes shorter-is-larger.
Teach 'annexing zeros is value-preserving' (0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700) only after the meaning is understood, never as a rote substitute for place-value reasoning.
Avoid teaching 'add zeros then compare as whole numbers' as the primary method; rules unsupported by place-value understanding are forgotten and can mask the misconception.

A length model or number line (where size is shown by length) is the recommended visual here; the source synthesis prefers length over volume/3D models for this topic. This is a stated preference for showing decimal magnitude, not a universal claim that other media cannot teach.

A static aligned chart or single shaded grid is a reference/scaffold: it may support reading or checking a comparison but does not by itself provide the repeated ragged-case practice with feedback that builds the comparison skill.

Multiple-choice/ordering/true-false questions with distractors built from longer-is-larger and shorter-is-larger can diagnose which faulty rule a child uses, but recognising the right option does not by itself build place-value insight; pair any quizzing with construction and justification.
Scope: Year 5 expectation is to read, write, order and compare numbers with up to three decimal places; extend from hundredths to thousandths deliberately.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the worked examples: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5 is correct; 0.312 and 0.38 share 3 tenths, and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) < 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 is correct (seven tenths = seventy hundredths). 0.87 > 0.4, 0.9 > 0.11, and 0.45 > 0.405 are correct. Ordering 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 gives 3.14 < 3.142 < 3.2. Grid counts: 0.4 = 4 columns = 40 squares; 0.38 = 38 squares. No arithmetic errors found.

Coherence fix applied: feedback referring to 0.4 vs 0.87, 0.9 vs 0.11 and 0.45 vs 0.405 now has matching learnerActions in Activity 1, because the main ordering set 0.4/0.38/0.312/0.5 can be ordered correctly by a shorter-is-larger learner and therefore does not reveal that misconception on its own.

Source verification is mixed in the original row: the SMART/Victoria synthesis claim is marked verified; the Durkin & Rittle-Johnson / Roell et al. / Steinle & Stacey synthesis claim and the DfE National Curriculum claim are marked unverified. The Durkin-synthesis claim is reused as a sourceClaim because it directly supports the metacognitive-naming principle, but its verification status was not upgraded here.

The original artefact wording asserting that a conversation or 3D model offers 'no spatial gain' and that a static picture 'cannot' teach has been softened to scoped affordances/limits; comparative necessity is a catalog preference, not established efficacy.
The length-over-volume preference is carried from the source synthesis as a recommendation for this topic, not as proof that volume/3D representations cannot teach decimal comparison.

probeDeeper: You placed 0.38 relative to 0.4 — which has more tenths? Does having more digits always mean bigger?
A friend says 0.9 is smaller than 0.11 because 11 is more than 9. What would you tell them?
Is 0.5 bigger or smaller than 0.45? What about 0.5 and 0.500?
How could you use this number line to check your whole order is right?
assess.correctAnswer: 0.312 < 0.38 < 0.4 < 0.5. Reasoning by place value: 0.312 and 0.38 have 3 tenths (smaller), and 0.312 (3 tenths 1 hundredth) is less than 0.38 (3 tenths 8 hundredths); 0.4 and 0.5 have 4 and 5 tenths. 0.7 = 0.70 — seven tenths equals seventy hundredths; the trailing zero does not change the value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-is-larger: 'more digits means bigger — 0.38 is more than 0.4 because 38 is bigger than 4', treating the digits after the point as a whole number.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the length model — 0.38 is shorter than 0.4 — and reason in place value: '0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'. Use ragged decimals; name and inhibit the whole-number rule. Reteach comparison of same-length decimals first.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks 0.312 and/or 0.38 as the largest; orders by digit count rather than by tenths.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (fraction-thinking): 'the shorter one is bigger — 0.4 beats 0.87 because sharing among 4 gives more than among 87', reading 0.4 as 1/4 and 0.87 as 1/87.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate decimal place value from denominator-size reasoning: 0.4 is four tenths, 0.87 is eight tenths and seven hundredths, so 0.87 is bigger; show both on the length model. Reteach decimal comparison from place value.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the shorter decimal as larger and justifies with a sharing/denominator analogy.

errorPatterns.pattern: Shorter-is-larger (tenths>hundredths): 'tenths are bigger than hundredths, so 0.4 is bigger than 0.87' — over-applying a partial truth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare place by place from the left: 0.87 has more tenths than 0.4, so it wins before hundredths matter; grids/length model make it visible. Reteach highest-place-first comparison.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct on pure tenth-vs-hundredth cases but wrong when the hundredths total exceeds the tenths gap (0.4 vs 0.87); may also mis-order fractions by denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Annexing a zero changes the value — '0.7 and 0.70 are different, 0.70 is bigger (or smaller)'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 7 tenths = 70 hundredths on a grid and equal lengths on the line; trailing zeros fill to equal length without changing size. Reteach place-value equivalence.

responseLevels.gap: Orders by number of digits (longer- or shorter-is-larger) or compares the tails as whole numbers; denies 0.7 = 0.70. Ragged decimals are mis-ordered.
responseLevels.full: Orders ragged decimals correctly by comparing the highest place value first, justifies in place-value language ('0.38 is 3 tenths 8 hundredths, less than 4 tenths'), knows 0.7 = 0.70, and transfers the method to thousandths and to counterexample pairs like 0.9 vs 0.11.
responseLevels.partial: Compares same-length decimals correctly but slips on ragged decimals, or reaches the right order by annexing zeros without explaining place value — executes a rule without the highest-place-first reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these in order from smallest to largest and show me how you decided: 0.4, 0.38, 0.312, 0.5. Then tell me — is 0.7 the same size as 0.70, and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: These are RAGGED decimals, so faulty rules cannot hide. A longer-is-larger child ranks 0.312 or 0.38 as largest ('more digits'). A shorter-is-larger child ranks 0.4/0.5 as largest for the wrong reason and mis-orders 0.312 vs 0.38, or claims 0.4 > 0.5-style errors on other pairs; watching the justification reveals whether it is the fraction-analogy or the tenths>hundredths route. The 0.7 vs 0.70 tier catches the belief that annexing a zero changes value. Same-length pairs would let every faulty rule pass — these do not.
